I don' t know about you all, but there is nothing worse than remembering that you typed a script or a command and cannot remember what it was and being too lazy to rethink and retype it. This is where bash history control comes into play. You can also make this more complex to keep all history in archived files, but here is the basics for rocking a combined long history file.

# don't put duplicate lines or lines starting with space in the history.
# See bash(1) for more options
# HISTCONTROL=ignoreboth

# append to the history file, don't overwrite it
shopt -s histappend

# for setting history length see HISTSIZE and HISTFILESIZE in bash(1)
export HISTSIZE=100000
export HISTFILESIZE=100000

# After each command, append to the history file and reread it
export PROMPT_COMMAND="history -a; history -c; history -r; $PROMPT_COMMAND"

Noting of course that '#' is a comment.

Another thing this makes easy is the use of the ! operator. When looking at your history file via history.. for example....

<USER>@usertop:~/Documents/Research$ history | grep nohup
 1954 nohup live-server notes-app &>/dev/null &
 1956 nohup live-server todos-app &> /dev/null &
 1962 nohup live-server todo-app &> /dev/null &
 2075 nohup live-server hangman &> /dev/null &
 2361 history | grep nohup
 2362 nohup firefox &> /dev/null &
 2364 nohup firefox &> /dev/null &
 2407 history | grep nohup
<USER>@usertop:~/Documents/Research$ !2075
nohup live-server hangman &> /dev/null &
[1] 15441

The use of !<NUM> allows me to rerun that line from my history file, without having to copy and paste.
Bash History - Keep all history from all terminal emulators and store them in the order in which arguments were entered.

Another nice tip is you can rerun a previous command and replace the command.

[~]$ cat file
foo
[~]$ history | grep cat
 1535 cat /proc/cpuinfo 
 1677 cat id_dsa.pub 
 1744 cat update_keydb
 1748 cat test
 1749 cat network_detect.sh 
 1760 cat temp 
 1764 cat ma
 1765 cat make-list.sh 
 1812 cat parents_phone 
 1848 locate doomsday
 1953 cat /etc/pulse/default.pa 
 2004 cat file
 2005 history | grep cat
[~]$ !2004:s/file/output/
cat output
something

To use your example, you can run something like this, if instead of rerunning hangman you wanted to rerun notes-app but that command wasn't in your history...

!2075:s/hangman/notes-app/

[~]$ whoami

[~]$ !!
whoami

[~]$ cat file

[~]$ echo $?
0
[~]$ cat foo
cat: foo: No such file or directory
[~]$ echo $?
1

Just some more tips to toss out there.
